title: Handle cancelled events from iCal feeds
description:
The iCal ingestion pipeline currently imports events even when they are cancelled. Cancellation can appear in two ways:

1. iCal standard: STATUS:CANCELLED property on the VEVENT
2. Source-specific: title contains '*** Cancelled ***' (seen with AFCEA Belvoir Eventbrite feed)

The QA agent should detect events with these signals and either skip them during ingestion or flag/hide them automatically.

Example: AFCEA Belvoir August 2026 Luncheon *** Cancelled *** (guid: 653c72128c89e69b95fb01687e369936) — was manually hidden via overlay on 2026-08-24.

Suggested approach:
- During iCal processing, check VEVENT STATUS:CANCELLED and skip those events
- Also filter titles matching case-insensitive pattern like '\*\*\* cancel' 
- For already-imported cancelled events, the QA agent should identify and hide them via overlay
close_reason: Closed

title: SEO: per-event landing pages that route users to the primary source
description: Every event links straight out (events_by_day.html:21), so the site has no indexable URL for any individual event and cannot rank for long-tail queries like 'kubernetes meetup arlington'. The homepage ItemList JSON-LD (homepage.html:55-106) is also ineligible for Google event rich results: items lack their own url on this domain, a full PostalAddress, and endDate.
design:
HARD CONSTRAINT: this site sends users to primary sources immediately and must not become a 'roach motel' calendar. Design rules, all required:

1. List pages keep linking directly out. events_by_day.html:21 is unchanged - the event TITLE always points at the organizer's URL, target=_blank.
2. The event page is a SEARCH LANDING PAGE, not a step in the site's own click path. It serves people arriving from Google who had no direct path to intercept.
3. Internal discovery is via a low-prominence permalink (a '#' glyph or the timestamp) beside the title, blog-permalink style. Crawlers follow it; users who want the event never click it. Orphan pages do not rank, so some internal link is required - the resolution is prominence, not presence.
4. On the event page the primary source link is THE primary action: above the fold, largest affordance, organizer's real hostname visible. No redirect interstitial, no click wrapper, no signup wall - a direct href.
5. Do NOT republish the organizer's description (available at calendars.py:231). That is both the substitution behavior we object to and duplicate content that would get the page filtered. Show facts only: when, where, who, categories.
6. Earn the page's existence with information the source does not have: also_published_by (which other groups list this event), a per-event .ics download, category cross-links, and persistence after the source link rots. Pairs with the archive work in the sibling issue.
7. Event JSON-LD: url points at our page (that is what earns the rich result); the source goes in offers.url, which is where Google routes 'register' clicks anyway. Include startDate, endDate, full PostalAddress, organizer, eventAttendanceMode, eventStatus.

Considered and rejected: anchor IDs on existing week/month pages. Honest and nearly free, but Google rarely ranks a fragment URL independently and per-event Event schema cannot attach cleanly to a 40-event page. Roughly a tenth of the upside.
acceptance_criteria: /events/<slug>/ pages freeze for every current event, carry valid Event structured data, appear in the sitemap, and are reachable only via the low-prominence permalink. Outbound behavior on all list pages is byte-identical to before except for the added permalink. Event descriptions from feeds are not republished.
close_reason: Closed

title: SEO: keep past month and week pages instead of letting them 404
description: get_upcoming_months() (app.py:629) derives months from current events only, and get_upcoming_weeks(12) bounds weeks the same way. Past month and week pages stop being generated and their URLs start 404ing, so accumulated links and rankings for e.g. /2026/6/ die on a monthly schedule.
acceptance_criteria: Past month and week pages stay frozen as archives, appear in the sitemap with an honest lastmod and changefreq never, and are reachable by an internal link. No previously-published URL 404s after a rebuild.
notes:
Investigated; needs a design decision before implementation. Confirmed the harm is real: site_generator_stack.py:52 deploys with 'aws s3 sync build/ --delete', so a month page that stops being generated is actively deleted from the bucket and returns a hard 404.

Why this is not a small fix: there is no historical event data anywhere in the pipeline. pipeline.py:304 and :328 drop events with event_date < today at ingest, and the ical cache only ever holds what the organizer's feed currently advertises - once an event passes, the source feed drops it and calgen has already discarded it. So past month/week pages cannot be rebuilt from anything on disk.

The weekly /updates roundups looked like an existing archive, but updates.py's module docstring rules that out going forward: as of 2026-08-12 roundups list the events ADDED that week, not the events HAPPENING that week. Only pre-2026-08-12 posts are 'what happened' snapshots.

The build is ephemeral CodeBuild (site_generator_stack.py BUILDSPEC) regenerating _data from a DynamoDB export each run, so any archive needs new persistent storage (S3 object or DynamoDB items) plus pipeline merge logic plus freezer generators plus a stack change for permissions.

Options put to the user 2026-08-13:
  a) Real archives - persist past events to a new store; accumulates from the change forward, cannot recover history already lost.
  b) Archive stubs - calgen enumerates every month/week from site launch to today and emits a 200 page saying the events have passed, linking to /updates and current listings. No new storage; deterministic; thin, so noindex+follow to preserve link flow without indexing near-duplicates.
  c) Accept the 404s.

Rejected as unworkable: scoping the s3 sync --delete to spare past paths. --exclude applies to source and destination alike, so sparing /2026/8/ from deletion would also stop it updating while it is still the current month, and the pattern cannot distinguish past from current.
IMPLEMENTED as variant A (publisher-side), per user 2026-08-13. The earlier 'needs new persistent storage' framing was wrong: _updates/ is already a DynamoDB export (export_dynamo_to_calgen.py:152), so the durable store already existed.

Publisher (updates_publisher/app.py): added _next_week_bounds, _events_in_week, _archive_item. Each Wednesday run now also writes ARCHIVE#<week_id>/SK=META for the FOLLOWING ISO week, computed from the events.json it already fetches - no new source, no new fetch, no IAM change. Guarded on today (not publish_date) so a backdated manual re-run cannot overwrite a good capture with an empty one.
Export: ARCHIVE items land in _archive/{week_id}.yaml. by_prefix is generic over PK prefix and filters SK==META, so no scan change was needed.
calgen: new archive.py (get_archived_weeks/week/events, merge_events). Week and month routes merge live + archived, live winning on conflict. get_all_week_ids/get_all_months drive the freezer and sitemap so past pages keep building.
Templates: archive-notice on past week/month pages; permalinks withheld from archived events since /events/ pages exist only for current events.
Also fixed a pre-existing bug the archive exposed: month prev/next nav linked to months that were never frozen (has_prev/has_next now gate it).

Known limits, by design: coverage starts when archiving starts - months already lost stay lost; a capture is taken up to a week ahead, so events added after it are missing (same fidelity the weekly email has). Variant B (site generator refreshes archives every build) closes that gap but needs a table write permission on the CodeBuild role.

title: MCP tools for reviewing and approving submissions
description:
The MCP server can create content but cannot see or act on the moderation queue, so triaging submissions requires the /edit UI. Add tools mirroring the REST admin routes: list_pending_submissions, get_submission, approve_submission (with optional trust_submitter), reject_submission, and list/trust/untrust_submitter.

Promotion logic currently lives in routes/admin.py, which the MCP Lambda does not bundle. Move it into db.py so the REST handlers and MCP share one implementation rather than growing a second copy of the approval rules.

Accepted trust boundary: MCP is IAM-authed for trusted agents and has no per-user admin check, unlike the REST routes. Confirmed acceptable — the endpoint already exposes add_single_event and set_overlay, so this is consistent with the existing boundary.
acceptance_criteria: An agent can list the pending queue, inspect a draft, approve it (optionally trusting the submitter), and reject it; approval promotes to EVENT#/GROUP# and marks the draft approved exactly as the REST route does; approval logic exists in one place; trusted submitters can be listed, added, and revoked.

title: Email the admin on every event submission
description: Send ross@karchner.com an immediate email whenever an event or group is submitted, complementing the daily queue digest in NextOpsStack. Auto-published submissions from trusted submitters are included, since those never reach the queue and the mail is the only signal they happened.
acceptance_criteria: Every submission path emails the admin; the mail names the event, submitter, and whether it is queued or already published; Reply-To is the submitter; an SES failure never fails the submission.
close_reason: Implemented and deployed; verified no send failures in production logs after two live submissions

title: Trusted submitters: auto-approve future submissions
description:
Add a 'trust this submitter' option to the approval flow. Once trusted, that person's later event submissions skip the moderation queue and publish immediately.

Trust is keyed by normalized email, which is the only stable identity across both auth paths (magic-link submitters have submitter_id 'magiclink:<email>' and no Cognito sub). This is safe because the magic-link flow proves control of the address before a submission is accepted — an attacker cannot submit as a trusted address without receiving that address's mail.

Auto-approved submissions still write a DRAFT record for the audit trail, then immediately promote and mark APPROVED with an automated reviewer, so the queue history stays complete and the EVENT# write triggers the usual rebuild.
acceptance_criteria: Approving with the trust box ticked records the submitter as trusted; that submitter's next event submission publishes without entering the queue and is visible in history as auto-approved; admins can list and revoke trusted submitters; untrusted submitters are unaffected; group submissions still require review.
close_reason: Implemented and verified in production: trust checkbox on approve, auto-approval of trusted submitters' events, admin list/revoke UI, 37 new tests

title: Newsletter opt-in checkbox on the event submission form
description:
Add a 'sign me up for the weekly newsletter' checkbox to the event submission form. When ticked, subscribe the submitter to the SES contact list.

No double opt-in confirmation email is needed here: the magic-link flow (or Cognito) has already proven the submitter controls that address, which is exactly what the newsletter confirmation link exists to establish. Subscribing directly avoids making the user confirm the same address twice in one flow.
acceptance_criteria: Ticking the box subscribes the submitter to the dctech topic on the newsletter contact list; leaving it unticked subscribes nobody; an SES failure does not fail the event submission.

title: Migration created ~31 duplicate events under mismatched guid schemes
description:

Same logical event, different key, so the collision check never fired and both copies were imported.

The migration report at the time ('62 copied verbatim') therefore understated the problem — roughly half of those 62 were duplicates of events that already existed under a calgen guid.

Surfaced as 'Also published by None' on the site: calgen's remove_duplicates merged the pair at render time and credited the duplicate's group, which was null for manual events.

Fixed 2026-08-02: 31 redundant records deleted (backed up to .backup-predecom-20260802/deleted-duplicate-events.json), keeping the calgen-canonical record of each pair. Legitimate co-publishing between iCal groups was deliberately left intact.
acceptance_criteria: No two EVENT# records share a title+date with no group. Any future migration reconciles on canonical event identity, not raw guid.

title: Cognito pool is taking sustained signup spam
description:
As of 2026-08-02, 51 of 66 accounts in us-east-1_8Ay4dTt8j were UNCONFIRMED, all created within about six days. The pattern is automated abuse, not real signups:

  - dot-injected Gmail aliases: l.i.z.a.g.ey.e.r.ma.n@gmail.com, r.ad.t.ech.mom.o@gmail.com, n.o.kia.fl.o.of.22@gmail.com
  - spoofed corporate domains: questions@valvesoftware.com, paypal@wwt.it
  - unrelated org domains: yuroktribe.nsn.us, leacounty.net, lift-texas.net

Only ~15 accounts are confirmed. The pool has selfSignUpEnabled with the hosted UI publicly reachable at login.dctech.events, so anything can register. Each signup also triggers a Cognito verification email through the SES identity, which puts the domain's sending reputation at risk if bounce rates climb.

The new weekly pruner (dctech-events-next-cleanup-unconfirmed-users) clears them after 7 days, so this is contained but not prevented. Its MAX_DELETIONS guard is set to 1000 to avoid blocking on this volume.

Options: enable the Cognito advanced-security / bot detection features, put WAF in front of the hosted UI, or turn off self-signup and invite admins manually.

## Context
Found while re-creating the pruning job that was lost when dctech-events-api was deleted. Worth checking SES bounce/complaint rates for the dctech.events identity too.
acceptance_criteria: Either signup abuse is being blocked at the edge, or a conscious decision is recorded that pruning alone is sufficient.
notes:
Timing analysis settles what this is. Unconfirmed signups arrive 4-52 seconds apart across wholly unrelated domains (accountspayable@cbwm.org, questions@valvesoftware.com, jberling@yuroktribe.nsn.us within seconds of each other); 16 of 50 consecutive pairs are under 3 minutes. That is machine-paced, and the plausible-looking addresses are harvested third-party addresses, not registrations by their owners.

So the abuse is using Cognito as an email relay: the victims are the address owners, who receive unsolicited verification mail from dctech.events. That is what drives the complaint rate (0.07% against AWS's 0.1% review threshold), and it is why prevention beats pruning — pruning cannot unsend an email.

A PreSignUp trigger is now deployed in AUDIT mode (ENFORCE=false) in NextCognitoStack. Validated against the real pool export: 0 false positives on all 15 confirmed users, catches 19 of 51 unconfirmed (37%) via gmail dot-injection and disposable domains. It cannot catch the remaining 63% because those addresses are genuinely well-formed — only rate limiting can.

Next: (1) review audit logs, then set ENFORCE=true; (2) add WAF rate-based rules on the login.dctech.events hosted UI, which is now the primary control rather than a fallback.
close_reason: Resolved by closing public sign-ups (AllowAdminCreateUserOnly=true, deployed 2026-08-08) — the SignUp endpoint bots were hitting is now rejected outright. Verified with a live SignUp call returning NotAuthorizedException.

The old dctech-events-api stack ran dctech-events-cleanup-unconfirmed-users on cron(0 2 ? * SUN *), deleting unconfirmed users from the shared pool us-east-1_8Ay4dTt8j. It last ran 2026-08-01 and was removed when that stack was deleted during decommissioning.

title: Normalize invisible Unicode in event titles
description:
Event titles arriving from iCal feeds can contain zero-width and other invisible Unicode characters. Left in place they break two things:

- skip_phrases matching, since a title with a zero-width space no longer matches the configured phrase
- duplicate detection, since are_events_duplicates in packages/calgen/src/calgen/pipeline.py compares titles exactly, and calculate_event_hash in event_utils.py folds the title into the guid — so the same event can churn guids or fail to dedupe

Upstream strips these characters in event_utils.py before hashing and in pipeline.py before comparison.

## Context
Behaviour exists in the now-archived rosskarchner/calgen at origin/main (commit 3c9246e, 'Fix invisible Unicode chars breaking skip_phrases filtering and duplicate detection'), fetchable from ~/projects/calgen. Note this changes guids for any affected event, so expect one-time churn: the aggregator will write new EVENT# items and prune the old ones. Upstream also ships tests/test_unicode_normalization.py worth porting alongside.
acceptance_criteria: Titles differing only by invisible characters produce the same guid and dedupe against each other; skip_phrases matching is unaffected by them.

title: Port skip_phrases group filtering into calgen
description:
Groups can declare skip_phrases to drop matching events from their feed. The vendored calgen ignores the field entirely, so those events publish. _groups/nvtc.yaml sets:

    skip_phrases:
      - COMMUNITY TUESDAYS AT REFRACTION

and roughly 15 such events are currently live on dctech.events; the pre-cutover site filtered them.

Upstream implements the match in packages/calgen/src/calgen/pipeline.py during event processing, case-insensitively against the event title.

## Context
Behaviour exists in the now-archived rosskarchner/calgen at origin/main (commit ce08c53), fetchable from ~/projects/calgen. Blocked by the db.py read bug — until that is fixed the field never reaches calgen even if the matching logic is ported.
acceptance_criteria: Events whose titles match a group's skip_phrases are absent from _data/all_events.json and the built site. The nvtc 'Community Tuesdays at Refraction' events stop appearing.
notes: Working as intended, with a correction to this ticket's premise. The nvtc feed publishes 2 'Community Tuesdays at Refraction' copies and skip_phrases now drops both. The 13 that remain on the site are source='recurring' — a curated RECURRING# definition expanded over 90 days — which group-level skip_phrases does not (and should not) touch. That is exactly why the phrase was configured: suppress the feed duplicates, keep the curated series. Live site now shows 13, matching the pre-cutover site's 13. The ticket's '~15 such events show' figure came from a grep that conflated occurrences.

title: Heading level skip on empty-results category/location pages
description: partials/sidebar.html uses bare h3 for 'Category'/'Month' with no h2 of its own -- it relies on the main content supplying one first (normally true via events_by_day.html's h2.day-heading). A category or location page with zero matching events renders only a 'No events found' paragraph with no heading, so the DOM order becomes h1 -> h3, skipping a level. Fix: give the sidebar its own h2, or demote it to h4 unconditionally.

The sidebar (aside) is a sibling section to main, not nested under it -- giving it its own h2 is correct in both cases: with events (h1 -> h2 day-heading -> ... -> h2 sidebar, two sibling top-level sections) and on empty-results pages (h1 -> h2 sidebar, no skip at all). The bead's alternative (demote to h4 unconditionally) would only have fixed the has-events case and made the empty-results skip worse (h1 straight to h4, a two-level skip instead of one). Updated the matching CSS selector (.sidebar-section h3 -> h2) so the small-caps label styling carries over unchanged. Committed in 44d5a91.

title: No focus management after the magic-link page-state swap
description: submission.js and correction.js's stripTokenFromUrl silently rewrites the URL and swaps #link-request to the actual form, but focus stays wherever it was -- typically nowhere, since the page just finished loading from an emailed link. A screen-reader or keyboard user gets no cue the page changed state. Fix: move focus to the revealed form's first field after the swap.

Deployed; verified live via curl that both pages load the updated JS with no syntax errors (node -c against the fetched files).

title: Recurring-event caveat is locked behind a hover-only title tooltip

title: Factor a shared PythonLambda CDK construct
description: CDK Lambda-construction boilerplate (runtime=PYTHON_3_12, timeout, handler path) is repeated 14 times across 9 stack files: ops_stack.py, api_stack.py, newsletter_stack.py, updates_stack.py, ical_aggregator_stack.py, qa_agent_stack.py, site_generator_stack.py, cognito_stack.py, and (until this session) discovery_agent_stack.py. A shared construct factory removes 5-8 repeated lines per call site and centralizes the next Python runtime bump.
notes:
Investigated, did NOT implement — leaving open rather than risking a botched deploy across live production stacks.

Confirmed the repetition: 13 lambda_.Function(...) call sites (not 14 — the bead's count likely included the now-deleted discovery agent stack) across 9 files: ical_aggregator_stack.py, api_stack.py (x2), site_generator_stack.py (x2), updates_stack.py (x2), cognito_stack.py, ops_stack.py (x2, already using a **log_defaults dict for its LogGroup calls — the most converged of the bunch), qa_agent_stack.py, newsletter_stack.py (x3).

The real risk, and why I stopped short of writing code: CDK's CloudFormation logical ID for a resource is derived from its full construct-path (scope + construct_id), hashed. If the shared "construct" is implemented as an actual `Construct` subclass (e.g. `class PythonLambda(Construct): ... lambda_.Function(self, "Resource", ...)`), every call site's underlying `AWS::Lambda::Function` gets a NEW logical ID (an extra path segment is inserted), which CloudFormation would read as delete-old/create-new — a real Lambda replacement (brief downtime, a changed physical function name/ARN anything referencing it by ARN would need updating, e.g. QaAgentStack's CalendarQcRuntime role trust, or the orchestration stack's Step Functions task references) across stacks including two I already touched and verified working this session (NextApiStack, NextQaAgentStack).

The safe version is a plain FACTORY FUNCTION, not a Construct class — `def python_lambda(scope, construct_id, *, ...): return lambda_.Function(scope, construct_id, ...)` — passing the original scope/construct_id straight through with no new nesting level, so the logical ID is byte-identical to today's. That part I'm confident about. What stopped me from just doing it: making 13 call sites' LogGroup children match this too requires each site's *existing* LogGroup construct id preserved exactly (they're inconsistent today — most use `logs.LogGroup(self, "SomeExplicitLogGroup", ...)` with a hand-picked name unrelated to the function's own construct_id; ops_stack.py's two do `**log_defaults`; some pass memory_size, some don't; some have log retention already set per bead next_dctech_events-3sd's fix, others don't yet — see that bead) — getting a shared signature that reproduces all 13 exactly, verified via `cdk diff` on every touched stack showing zero replacements, is real work I didn't want to rush at the tail end of a long batch.

Recommend as a dedicated follow-up: write the factory function, convert ONE low-risk stack first (ops_stack.py, already closest to converged and lowest production impact), confirm `cdk diff` shows no replacement, deploy, then repeat per-stack rather than all 9 in one pass.
close_reason:
Plan approved by user, implemented exactly as the fork's investigation recommended: cdk_next/constructs_lib/python_lambda.py, a plain factory function (not a Construct subclass — a subclass inserts its own construct-path segment, changing the CFN logical ID CDK derives from that path, which reads as delete-old/create-new; calling lambda_.Function(scope, construct_id, ...) directly with no extra nesting keeps the logical ID byte-identical). Named constructs_lib, not constructs, to avoid shadowing the real `constructs` PyPI package imported everywhere as `from constructs import Construct`.

Piloted on ops_stack.py (the fork's own recommended lowest-risk, most-converged stack) — both Lambdas converted, log_group_id passed explicitly per call site since existing log group ids don't derive from the function's own construct_id. Verified via `cdk diff` before deploying: zero resource replacements, only routine code-hash churn plus an SES wildcard-grant fix (resources=["*"] -> the dctech.events identity ARN, the same class of fix already applied everywhere else this session, found and fixed while in this file). Deployed NextOpsStack — UPDATE_COMPLETE, function names/ARNs unchanged — and confirmed live via a direct invoke of the cleanup function (ran successfully, no errors).

Stopped after this one stack, per the fork's own advice: convert the remaining 8 call sites incrementally with the same cdk-diff verification each time, not all at once in one pass.

title: Split packages/calgen/src/calgen/app.py into a routes/ package
description: app.py is a 1,507-line monolith with 31 @app.route handlers and every helper inlined (event filtering, day-grouping, feed generation, newsletter, sitemap), despite cdk_next/lambda_src/api/ already establishing a routes/ package pattern in this same repo. Splitting by concern (events/feeds/newsletter/admin-adjacent) would cut the repo's largest file by 60-70% per module.
notes:
Investigated, did NOT implement — left open given size and time already spent in this batch, not because it looks infeasible.

Structure confirmed: all 31 @app.route handlers live inside one _register_routes(app) function (closures over `app`, called from create_app()), with ~20 module-level helper functions below them (get_events, get_categories, get_event_by_slug, filter_events_to_upcoming_days, prepare_events_by_day, _month_url, etc.) that the route closures call into. This is more tractable than it sounds: the helpers are already free-standing module-level functions, not nested closures, so they can move cleanly. Frozen-Flask discovers routes via app.url_map regardless of which module registered them, so splitting registration into multiple `register(app)` calls (one per resource-group module, mirroring cdk_next/lambda_src/api/routes/'s existing pattern in this same repo) is safe for the freeze step.

The real constraint, found by checking test coverage before touching anything: several tests monkeypatch specific calgen.app module attributes directly — e.g. test_breadcrumb_jsonld.py does `monkeypatch.setattr('calgen.app.get_events', ...)` and `'calgen.app.get_categories'`; test_event_page_jsonld.py does `'calgen.app.get_event_by_slug'`; test_upcoming_window.py imports `filter_events_to_upcoming_days`/`prepare_events_by_day` directly from calgen.app. A split MUST re-export these specific names from app.py (`from calgen.routes.events import get_events` etc.) rather than just deleting them from app.py's namespace, or those monkeypatches silently stop taking effect (setattr succeeds on a name that's no longer what the route code actually calls) and the tests would pass for the wrong reason or fail confusingly. This is doable but requires auditing every monkeypatch/direct-import across all 266 tests against the final re-export list before considering it done, not just running the suite once at the end and trusting a pass.

Recommend as a dedicated follow-up, not squeezed into a larger batch: grep tests/ for every `calgen.app.X`/`from calgen.app import X` reference first, treat that list as the required re-export surface, split by resource group (events/feeds/newsletter/sitemap/updates — the natural boundaries the route list already falls into), then run the full 266-test suite and confirm nothing changed from a real check to a silent no-op.

title: Two EVENT# rows store an unparsed date string
description:
Two rows hold date='June 6th 2025' and time='6pm' — free text where every other
row holds ISO-8601. Found 2026-08-27 while checking cpp.6 for evidence; they are
2 of 351 EVENT# rows.

  5b77f96cd548d3eab47d82af72ed25ae   manual   date='June 6th 2025' time='6pm'
  14fe7799-eecd-5457-a883-74178e832f5b  manual  date='June 6th 2025' time=None

Both are the same event ("Technology CFO Awards", NVTC), so they are also a
duplicate pair. Both are from June 2025 and absent from the site: calgen's
load_single_events runs the string through dateparser, resolves it, and then
drops it as past. So there is no reader-visible effect.

WHY IT IS STILL WORTH A LINE. put_event writes GSI1SK/GSI4SK from the date
verbatim, so these rows sort as if they were in the year "June". Any range query
over GSI4 — which is how get_all_events bounds a month or "today forward" —
treats them as far-future. That is exactly what made my cpp.6 evidence check
produce a false positive: `date >= '2026-08-27'` is true for the string "June 6th
2025" because "J" sorts after "2". A future date-range query could be misled the
same way, and the failure is silent.

Cause is upstream of the table: db.build_event_draft_data and MCP
add_single_event both take `date` as given without parsing or validating it.
calgen tolerates it because load_single_events parses defensively; DynamoDB does
not, because a sort key is a string.

FIX, in rough order of value:
  1. Validate on the way in — reject or normalize a non-ISO date in
     build_event_draft_data and add_single_event. That is the real fix and it
     stops the next one.
  2. Repair or delete these two rows. They are a past duplicate pair, so
     deleting both via MCP delete_single_event is defensible; they are also
     harmless where they are.
close_reason: Closed

title: Junk overlays written as booleans by an old admin form
description:
Two manual events carried the overlay {'title': True, 'hidden': True,
'categories': True} — boolean flags where values belong. Found on 2026-08-27
while deploying the overlay work, and cleared through the new DELETE
/api/admin/events/{guid}/overlay route:

  8dd82dbd997524b50e3757e2296b8ac8  CyberTalks 2026            2026-02-19
  26fc54aaebd278cfffbb4eea5e922ac9  Test CORS Approve Event    2026-03-15

No site impact: both are past-dated and already carried a top-level
hidden=True, so the pipeline dropped them regardless. They mattered only
because step 4 made overlays apply to manual events — before that they were
inert by accident rather than by intent.

Almost certainly written by the old forked admin form. The stranded template
cdk_next/lambda_src/api/templates/partials/admin_event_override_form.html has
`<input type="checkbox" name="hidden" value="true">` alongside text inputs, and
its route parsed form encoding, so a submit could produce truthy strings for
every named field. The second title ("Test CORS Approve Event") says test data.

WHAT THIS EXPOSES, and the actual reason to file it: db.check_overlay_fields
validates field *names* against OVERLAY_EDITABLE_FIELDS but not field *types*.
`{'title': True}` is accepted today. Worth adding type checks to
_validate_overlay_values in cdk_next/lambda_src/api/db.py — title/location/url
and friends are strings, hidden/all_day are bools, categories is a list of
strings. Cheap, and it is the difference between a UI bug being caught at the
boundary and being caught eight months later during a deploy.

Nothing else in the corpus is affected: the same scan found 22 events with
overlays and only these two were malformed.
close_reason: Closed

title: QC polish pass should correct improbable city/state pairs
description:
Ask the QC polish pass to catch locations whose city and state cannot both be
right — "Arlington, DC" (Arlington is in Virginia), "Bethesda, VA", "Reston,
MD".

WHY IT MATTERS: this is not cosmetic, unlike the doubled-city issue in
next_dctech_events-8so. `location_utils.extract_location_info` reads the
trailing `City, ST`, so a wrong state silently files the event under the wrong
region facet:

  extract_location_info("… Arlington, DC, Arlington, DC") -> ('Washington','DC')

The event then appears under /locations/washington-dc/ instead of Northern
Virginia, and a reader filtering by region never sees it.

HOW COMMON: rare. I scanned all 338 EVENT# items (2026-08-26) against a table
of DC-area cities and found exactly one:

  dd0d5c82  "DevFest DC 2026 - Build Edition"  (Google Developer Group DC)
            "3351 Fairfax Dr, 3351 Fairfax Drive, Arlington, DC, Arlington, DC"

Source is Meetup's own addressRegion, so this is upstream content error rather
than a pipeline bug — nothing to normalize, it needs judgement. Filed P3 on
frequency, not on impact: worth having as a standing check because it fails
silently, but it is not urgent at one event.

That one event is also half of the duplicate pair 8ea07ae7 / dd0d5c82, so the
triage pass may hide it before polish ever looks at it. Do not treat its
disappearance as evidence this is fixed.

IMPLEMENTATION: a rule in POLISH_PROMPT (cdk_next/agents/calendar_qc/prompt.py).
Needs care, because the prompt currently says:

  "never change a location to move an event between cities — that is the
   out-of-area pass's decision, not yours"

Correcting Arlington, DC -> Arlington, VA does not move the event; it labels
the same place correctly. The rule needs an explicit carve-out saying so, or
the model will read the existing caution and leave it alone. Keep the
prohibition on actually relocating an event.

Worth pairing with a deterministic check instead of or alongside the prompt: a
city -> state table for the DC metro is small, and a mismatch is a fact rather
than a judgement. A validator in the aggregator or the MCP's set_overlay path
would catch it without a model call. The scan that found this used ~26 cities.
close_reason: Closed

title: QC: duplicates that appear after approval are never re-checked
description:
An event that becomes a duplicate AFTER approval (feed edits its title/date into
collision) never re-enters the pending_qa queue, since the aggregator preserves
review_status on refresh. The corpus-comparison design catches new-vs-existing
but not this. Fix if it ever bites: a periodic full sweep ignoring the queue.
Not worth building without evidence it happens.

CHECKED 2026-08-27, no evidence found. Closed on this bead's own criterion.

Method: ran calgen's own are_events_duplicates over every future EVENT# row that
was approved, not already marked duplicate_of, and not hidden — 174 of 230
future events — across all pairs.

One pair matched, and it was a false positive in the check rather than a real
drift: both rows are "Technology CFO Awards" with date stored as the *string*
"June 6th 2025". A lexical `date >= today` filter admits them because "J" sorts
after "2". They are a June 2025 event, absent from the site (0 listings), and
calgen drops them at build time once dateparser resolves the string. Corrected
for that, the count is zero.

Worth knowing when this is revisited: even an unmarked duplicate pair is merged
at render anyway. calgen's remove_duplicates runs are_events_duplicates over the
whole corpus independently of duplicate_of, so post-approval drift costs a
missing explicit mark rather than a doubled listing. That lowers the stakes
enough that a periodic sweep would be tidying rather than fixing.

If evidence does turn up, the cheap version is a scheduled pass that queries
GSI5 for review_status=approved and re-runs the corpus comparison — no new index
needed. The expensive version, re-queueing on refresh, would put every edited
event back through the agent weekly.

Filed separately: next_dctech_events-eex, the two non-ISO date rows this turned
up.
close_reason: Closed

description: main.css's .event-permalink layers opacity: 0.35 on top of an already-light color token, landing around 1.6:1 against white -- below any WCAG threshold. title: Give events distinct social share images instead of one site-wide og:image
description: site/templates/base.html defaults og:image to one generic /static/images/og-image.png; event_page.html overrides title/description/og_title/og_description but never og_image -- every one of hundreds of distinct events shares one card image in search/social previews. Even a simple date/category-based generated card would improve CTR.
notes:
Leaving open — this needs a design decision before it's a mechanical fix, not something to pick unilaterally.

Real options, roughly in order of effort:
1. Cheapest: a small set of pre-made static images per category (site already has category slugs), swap og_image based on event.categories[0]. No new infra, ships in an hour, but still not per-event.
2. Genuinely per-event: generate a card at build time (site-generator CodeBuild already runs Python per build) — title + date + category rendered onto a template via Pillow, written to /static/og/{guid}.png, uploaded alongside the rest of the site. Real but bounded work: a new calgen build step, a font/template design decision, one more file per event in the S3 sync.
3. On-demand via a Lambda@Edge/CloudFront Function generating the image at request time — more moving parts, not obviously worth it for a mostly-static site that already rebuilds on every content change.

Recommend option 1 as a quick win now and option 2 as the real fix if it's worth the design time — but the actual image design (what it looks like) is a product/brand call, not something to guess at. Say the word on direction and I'll build it.

title: Raise or paginate the sitemap's week-page cap
description: packages/calgen/src/calgen/app.py's sitemap route calls get_all_week_ids(12), limiting the sitemap to the most recent 12 weeks. Older frozen week pages presumably still exist and serve, but age out of the sitemap, losing long-tail indexing for 'DC tech events week of [date]'-style queries a recurring local site could otherwise own. Fix: raise the cap or paginate the sitemap.
close_reason: Investigated; the bead's premise doesn't hold against current code, so no change made. get_all_week_ids(num_weeks=12) (packages/calgen/src/calgen/app.py) unions get_upcoming_weeks(12) with get_archived_weeks() -- and get_archived_weeks() (archive.py) returns every .yaml file under _archive/ unconditionally, with no cap anywhere in that path (confirmed no pruning logic in archive.py, and the DynamoDB export in export_dynamo_to_calgen.py dumps every ARCHIVE# item with no limit either). The '12' argument only bounds how many *upcoming* weeks get pre-built/listed before any event has landed in them -- it does not cap historical week pages, which are already all included via the archive union, in both the sitemap and the Frozen-Flask freezer generator (freeze.py's week_page() uses the identical call). So 'older frozen week pages... age out of the sitemap' does not actually happen with the current code; the long-tail SEO value the bead was after is already there. Raising the upcoming-side number would just add more pre-built future week pages with zero events yet (thin content), which cuts against SEO rather than helping it. Closing as investigated/no-op rather than guessing at a fix for a symptom that isn't reproducible from the code.

title: Magic-link KMS key: cost review, decided to keep as dedicated
description: Reviewed alternatives for the magic-link signing key's ~$1/mo fixed KMS cost: (1) keep the dedicated customer-managed key -- recommended: clean blast-radius boundary for the one auth-critical capability that depends on it, $1/mo is trivial next to the operational risk of touching a live signing key; (2) consolidate with another small-purpose key -- no natural partner exists today, nothing else in the stack uses a KMS HMAC key (the QC agent's new Tavily secret is Secrets Manager, not KMS); (3) use an AWS-managed key instead -- not viable, HMAC KeySpec (required for generate_mac/verify_mac) is only available on customer-managed KMS keys. Conclusion: no action for now. Revisit only if a second small-purpose signing/HMAC need appears and a shared key becomes worth the coupling.
close_reason: Already resolved when filed -- the bead itself documents the cost-alternatives review and its conclusion (keep the dedicated key, no action). Nothing further to do.
